Content:
Recall that a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: n] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] of [MATH: A] is a nonzero vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}] such that

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{v} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_{n-1} \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \ldots \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{v}_1 \xrightarrow{A- \lambda I} \mathbf{0},]

Content:
where [MATH: \mathbf{v}_{n-1}, \mathbf{v}_{n-2},\ldots, \mathbf{v}_{1} \neq \mathbf{0}.] In other words, [MATH: A-\lambda I] maps [MATH: \mathbf{v}] to [MATH: \mathbf{0}] in [MATH: n] steps. This is equivalent to the following:

Content:
[MATH: (A - \lambda I)^n \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
(A - \lambda I)^{n-1} \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
By the definition of the null space of a matrix, [MATH: (A - \lambda I)^k \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}] if and only if [MATH: \mathbf{v} \in \text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^k.]
This, in turn, means that a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: n] lies in [MATH: \text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^n] but not in [MATH: \text{Null}(A-\lambda I)^{n-1}.]

For example, suppose that a matrix [MATH: A] has the characteristic polynomial

Content:
[MATH: p(\lambda) = (5-\lambda)^6(\lambda-3)^2(\lambda+4)^5.]

Content:
In addition, let's assume the following:

Content:
- The nullity of [MATH: (A+4I)^3] equals [MATH: 2.]
- The nullity of [MATH: (A+4I)^4] equals [MATH: 3.]

If a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^{13}] consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of [MATH: A], how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank [MATH: 4] corresponding to the eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = -4?]

[MATH: (A + 4I)^4 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}
\qquad \textrm{and} \qquad
(A + 4I)^3 \mathbf{v} \neq \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Notice the following:

Content:
- We are given that [MATH: \text{Null}(A+4I)^3] has dimension [MATH: 2.] This means that the solutions to [MATH: (A +4I)^3 \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}] form a subspace of dimension [MATH: 2.]

Now, since [MATH: \text{Null}(A+4I)^3] is a subspace of dimension [MATH: 2] in [MATH: \text{Null}(A+4I)^4], which is a subspace of dimension [MATH: 3,] our basis can contain only [MATH: 1] vector that lies in [MATH: \text{Null}(A+4I)^4] but does not lie in [MATH: \text{Null}(A+4I)^3.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
For some [MATH: n\times n] matrices, it's possible to construct a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] consisting entirely of linearly independent eigenvectors of the matrix.

Content:
For example, the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [4|0|0; 0|2|1; 0|0|5]]

Content:
has eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1 = 5, \lambda_2 = 4,] and [MATH: \lambda_3 = 2,] with corresponding linearly independent eigenvectors

Content:
[MATH: [0; 1; 3]]
These eigenvectors form a basis of [MATH: \mathbb R^3.]

Content:
However, there exist [MATH: n\times n] matrices whose eigenvectors do not form a basis of [MATH: \mathbb R^n.]

Content:
For example, the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [4|0|0; 0|4|1; 0|0|4]]

Content:
has the single eigenvalue [MATH: {\color{black}\lambda=4}] of algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 3.] However, there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, namely

Content:
[MATH: [1; 0; 0]]

Content:
Since there are only two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we say that the geometric multiplicity of [MATH: {\color{black}\lambda=4}] equals [MATH: 2.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Forming a Basis Using Generalized Eigenvectors

Content:
So, not every [MATH: n\times n] matrix has the property that its eigenvectors form a basis of [MATH: \mathbb R^n.]

Content:
Despite this, we have the following theorem:

Content:
> For any real [MATH: n \times n] matrix, there is a basis of [MATH: \mathbb{R}^n] consisting of generalized eigenvectors of the matrix.

Content:
To illustrate, let's go back to our matrix
[MATH: [4|0|0; 0|4|1; 0|0|4]]

Content:
where the eigenvectors corresponding to the single eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda = 4] are

Content:
[MATH: [1; 0; 0]]

Content:
Remember that [MATH: \lambda = 4] has algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 3] and geometric multiplicity [MATH: 2.]

Content:
Now, it's easy to show that [MATH: A] has a generalized eigenvector of rank [MATH: 2] given by
